source.title: Understanding Inhibition Through Maximally Tense Images
source.authors: Christopher J. Hamblin; Srijani Saha; Talia Konkle; George A. Alvarez

record.tranche_reason: The paper tests whether superposition can produce misleading mixed attribution patterns, using toy networks and an image-model attribution-overlap analysis rather than the original neuron-interpretation method.
record.gate_note: The paper does not test whether canonical individual neurons respond to unrelated image categories. It does test whether capacity bottlenecks and attribution-selection choices produce patterns relevant to the superposition and measurement-dependence versions. The human MEI/MII prediction experiment and the attribution-completeness analyses do not directly measure polysemanticity, so they are not rows.
record.test_reason: The paper studies inhibition in vision models using maximally tense images. It invokes superposition to explain misleading excitation and inhibition attribution patterns. Neither the toy-model attribution matrices nor the InceptionV1 uniqueness metric measures whether individual neurons respond to several unrelated inputs. They also give no share of such neurons and no comparison across conditions that would change that share. The toy result shows interference attribution from irrelevant input features to output features. It is summed over the hidden layer, not per neuron. The uniqueness metric measures how often different units' top-attribution images overlap. Both are related constructs, recorded under fits_no_version. The L1-versus-L2 contrast concerns how images are selected for attribution, not whether a neuron counts as polysemantic, so it does not test V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The main conclusion is that maximally tense images and the new visualizations (±attribution inversions, the attribution atlas) expose inhibition's functional role. Superposition is a major obstacle because networks use negative weights to compress more features than units. A clean account of deep-layer inhibition likely needs monosemantic disentanglement.
record.recipe_differences: Uses layer-to-feature gradient attributions, toy networks implementing absolute value and XOR, and an image-overlap uniqueness analysis; it does not reproduce the original neuron-visualization method.
record.method_sensitivity: Attribution-image uniqueness changes with layer depth and with use of L1 versus L2 attribution norms.

fits_no_version.finding: In bottlenecked toy ReLU models (m=10, 8, 6 vs 12) computing abs and XOR, irrelevant input features produce large off-diagonal excitation and inhibition attributions to output features.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Superposition interference produces excitation and inhibition attributions from features irrelevant to the target output.

fits_no_version.finding: In deeper InceptionV1 layers, many units and k-means directions share the same high-attribution images, unlike MEIs. The L2 norm reduces this overlap relative to L1. Images high for at least 15 of 20 features show single concepts such as dog faces.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Attribution-selected images overlap across features in deep vision layers, consistent with superposed features loading onto many units.

record.problems: The toy models are small and synthetic. The InceptionV1 attribution-overlap result is presented mainly as evidence consistent with superposition, not as a causal demonstration that particular neurons encode unrelated features. Figure 8 does not provide numerical values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No directly relevant reported results were omitted. The human MEI/MII prediction experiment and completeness/correlation analyses were not extracted as rows because they do not measure polysemanticity or its prevalence.

untested.parts: Whether InceptionV1 or other vision neurons respond to unrelated inputs. The paper's MEI/MII pairing observation concerns inhibition, not mixed excitation.
Not addressed; no language models are studied.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise from superposition. The paper shows only interference attributions in toy models and overlap of attribution images.
Not addressed. SoLU and Top-k are mentioned only as other suppressive mechanisms.
Activation-range cutoffs and explanation scoring for neuron polysemanticity are not studied.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's links to V3 and V7 overstate the study. No row measures whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs, so no verdicts are given. The toy models replicate Toy Models of Superposition, which is not an original source here, and measure interference rather than polysemanticity.

versions.untested_parts: Whether vision-model neurons respond to several unrelated inputs, including the cited InceptionV1 neuron example.
Language models and MLP-neuron responses to unrelated tokens or contexts.

The toy models test superposition under bottlenecks, and the InceptionV1 analysis is consistent with shared attribution from interference; the paper does not establish that this mechanism causes polysemanticity across trained networks generally.
Polysemanticity without capacity pressure, including effects of initialization, regularization, or training noise.
Comparisons of activation functions, architectures, or regularization methods for polysemantic-neuron prevalence or performance cost.
Whether canonical polysemantic neurons, when examined with better tools, have one shared feature or related jobs rather than unrelated mixtures.
The paper compares attribution norms and examines layer depth, but does not compare activation-range cutoffs or explanation-scoring methods for classifying individual neurons as polysemantic.

rows.subject: absolute-value toy model (m=12)
rows.operation_detail: Measured positive and negative layer-to-output attributions for one-hot inputs and their negatives.
rows.measure: Off-diagonal positive and negative attribution in the input-feature/output-feature attribution matrix.
rows.value: The attribution matrix has positive attribution on the diagonal only and zero attribution elsewhere.
rows.note: The paper describes this as the disentangled model, able to compute the function exactly without feature interference.
rows.check: Control toy model. The attribution matrix is input feature × output feature, summed over hidden neurons, so it cannot show per-neuron polysemanticity. It is a related construct, not V3.

rows.subject: absolute-value toy model (m=10)
rows.operation_detail: Measured positive and negative layer-to-output attributions for one-hot inputs and their negatives.
rows.measure: Off-diagonal positive and negative attribution in the input-feature/output-feature attribution matrix.
rows.baseline: The m=12 model has attribution on the diagonal only.
rows.value: The attribution matrix shows off-diagonal attribution under the tighter hidden-dimension bottleneck.
rows.note: The paper says the off-diagonal attributions come from independent input features irrelevant to the output feature.
rows.check: Off-diagonal attribution under a bottleneck shows superposition interference, not that hidden neurons are polysemantic. This is a replication of Elhage et al. toy models. Move to fits_no_version.

rows.subject: XOR toy model (m=12)
rows.operation_detail: Measured positive and negative layer-to-output attributions for inputs with one or both elements of an XOR pair on.
rows.measure: Off-diagonal positive and negative attribution in the input-feature/output-feature attribution matrix.
rows.value: The disentangled model shows functionally relevant excitation and inhibition for the XOR output and no reported bottleneck-style off-diagonal attribution.
rows.note: In this model, excitation and inhibition for the same XOR output cancel for the [1,1] input.
rows.check: XOR control. This is functionally relevant inhibition, unrelated to neuron polysemanticity.

rows.subject: InceptionV1
rows.operation_detail: Compared uniqueness of selected images across features when selecting maximally exciting images.
rows.measure: Uniqueness U of images selected across features.
rows.value: U is near ceiling across layers.
rows.note: The text describes the curve as near ceiling; exact values are not stated.
rows.check: MEI uniqueness across units is a selection-overlap metric, not polysemanticity. It is a comparator for the attribution-selection rows. It also has no bearing on V7, which concerns classifying a neuron as polysemantic.

rows.subject: InceptionV1
rows.operation_detail: Compared uniqueness of selected images across features when selecting high-attribution images using the L1 norm.
rows.measure: Uniqueness U of images selected across features.
rows.baseline: MEI selections have uniqueness near ceiling across layers.
rows.value: Uniqueness decreases substantially in deeper layers.
rows.note: The paper interprets the overlap as consistent with many features having high attribution to the same images; values are plotted but not given numerically in the text.
rows.check: Decreasing uniqueness of L1 high-attribution images in deeper layers is attribution overlap across units. The authors call it only consistent with superposition. It does not measure neuron polysemanticity.

rows.subject: InceptionV1
rows.operation_detail: Compared uniqueness of selected images across features when selecting high-attribution images using the L2 norm.
rows.measure: Uniqueness U of images selected across features.
rows.baseline: MEI selections have uniqueness near ceiling across layers.
rows.value: The L2 measure mitigates the deeper-layer decrease in uniqueness somewhat compared with L1.
rows.note: The paper reports the same general deeper-layer overlap pattern but says it is somewhat mitigated by L2.
rows.check: L2 versus L1 is a choice of attribution image selection, not of how neurons are judged polysemantic. It is not V7.

rows.subject: InceptionV1
rows.operation_detail: Compared uniqueness of selected images across k-means features when selecting maximally exciting images.
rows.measure: Uniqueness U of images selected across features.
rows.value: The plotted MEI uniqueness curve is near ceiling across layers.
rows.note: The k-means-feature series is dotted; exact values are not stated.
rows.check: k-means directions are not neurons, and this is a selection-overlap metric. Values are read from the figure only.

rows.subject: InceptionV1
rows.operation_detail: Compared uniqueness of selected images across k-means features when selecting high-attribution images using the L1 norm.
rows.measure: Uniqueness U of images selected across features.
rows.baseline: MEI selections have uniqueness near ceiling across layers.
rows.note: The text describes deeper-layer decreases for MTIs and says the figure includes unit and k-means feature series; exact k-means curve values are not stated.
rows.check: Same as R10, for k-means directions, which are not neurons. Values are read from the figure only.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Bottlenecked toy networks and high-attribution image selection in deeper InceptionV1 layers
reader_labels.reason: Independent inputs produce off-diagonal attributions in bottlenecked toy models, and high-attribution image selections overlap across features in deeper layers; see R2-R4, R6-R8, and R10-R11, R13-R14.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: InceptionV1 attribution-overlap analysis across feature-selection measures and depth
reader_labels.reason: The observed overlap depends on selection: L2 mitigates the deeper-layer uniqueness decrease compared with L1, while MEIs remain near ceiling in uniqueness; see R9-R14.
